audience: Engineers familiar with relational tables and basic SQL learning SQLite's embedded model, transaction behavior and operational fit.
prerequisites: An application can send queries to a database. A relational table has rows and columns, and basic SQL SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE read or change those rows.
A transaction groups database work and ends with commit to accept it or rollback to discard it; the lesson defines its guarantees and concurrency limits.

objectives.description: Define SQLite as an embedded SQL database and trace in-process access to persistent local storage.
Choose SQLite based on data locality and access concurrency rather than an arbitrary user-count cutoff.
Explain SQLite storage classes/type affinity, STRICT tables and explicit constraint/foreign-key configuration.
Define SQLite ACID and explain transaction boundaries and the dependence of durability on storage and configuration.
Explain SQLite's one-writer rule, busy responses and short transaction/retry practices without equating it to one reader or one connection.
Explain rollback journaling, write-ahead logging, checkpoints and WAL concurrency/storage boundaries.
Explain query plans and indexes for SQLite, including workload-based choice and write/storage costs.
Explain SQLite backup consistency, active-file hazards, migrations and restore testing.
Integrate locality, write concurrency, correctness and recovery into an SQLite choice and recognize when to use a server database.

questions.question: Define embedded database and explain how an application uses SQLite to execute SQL and persist data. Contrast the process and network boundary with a separate database server. Does embedded mean in-memory only or no relational/transaction features? Compare an application-local dataset and a database that many application servers must update over a network. Explain why SQLite suits the first, what makes the second harder, and why user count or database size alone does not settle the choice. Does an SQLite file automatically synchronize separate devices?
criteria: SQLite is a database library linked into the application process; SQL executes through library calls rather than a required separate database server process and network request.
It can store relational data persistently in a local database file and supports transactions; embedded does not mean only an in-memory store or a key-value-only interface.
The application and environment own file access and operational responsibility; removing a server does not remove persistence or recovery concerns.
Local application data, embedded systems and suitable single-host services benefit from direct local access and no separate database service to deploy.

Multiple application servers needing a shared network database introduce access and concurrency requirements a client-server database is designed to coordinate; SQLite is not a substitute for that server protocol.

The decisive factors include where access occurs, concurrent writes and workload, rather than a universal maximum-user or dataset-size rule. An SQLite file does not automatically synchronize independent device copies.
criticalMisconceptions: SQLite requires a separate database server.
Embedded means data cannot survive application exit.
SQLite is only usable for toys or only for one end user.
Separate SQLite files automatically synchronize.

questions.question: Define SQLite type affinity and contrast ordinary tables with STRICT tables. Explain the roles of primary keys, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK and foreign keys; why should required values have explicit NOT NULL, and what must the application verify about foreign-key enforcement on its connections? Explain atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability for a group of SQLite changes. How do commit and rollback affect partial work, and why are constraints and correct transaction logic still needed? Explain why journaling/durability settings and storage behavior matter, and why rolling back the transaction does not undo an external action.
criteria: Ordinary SQLite tables use type affinity to guide conversion and storage rather than treating every declared type as an absolute column restriction; values have storage classes. STRICT tables enforce stricter supported type rules.

Primary keys identify rows, UNIQUE restricts duplicates, NOT NULL rejects missing values, and CHECK rejects false conditions. Express required-value rules explicitly with NOT NULL where needed rather than relying on a type declaration.

Foreign keys constrain references to related rows when enforcement is enabled; configure and verify PRAGMA foreign_keys for the application's connections rather than assuming declarations alone are enforced.
Typing and constraints enforce declared rules, not all business correctness; combining CHECK with NOT NULL matters when missing values must be invalid.
Atomicity commits the grouped database changes together or rolls them back; consistency preserves applicable declared constraints and correctly implemented invariants.
Isolation governs what concurrent transactions can observe and how writes are coordinated; it is not a promise that arbitrary application logic has no races or waits.
Durability concerns committed changes surviving the supported failures, with journaling, synchronization settings and reliable storage part of that guarantee; unsafe settings can weaken it.
Only database work inside the transaction is covered. An external network call or other side effect requires separate coordination and is not reversed by database rollback.
criticalMisconceptions: Every ordinary SQLite column rigidly enforces its declared type.
Declaring a foreign key guarantees enforcement on every connection.
Using transactions automatically validates every business rule.
SQLite commit durability is independent of storage and configuration.

questions.question: What does SQLite's one-writer-at-a-time rule mean when several connections are active? Define write contention and a busy result. Explain how short write transactions, bounded busy waits/retries and handling failed attempts help; why do these measures not produce multiple simultaneous writers or guarantee success? Contrast rollback-journal mode with SQLite write-ahead logging (WAL). Define a checkpoint and explain how WAL lets readers and a writer overlap while retaining a single writer. How can long readers affect checkpoint progress and WAL size, and what same-host/shared-file assumptions must be respected?
criteria: Multiple connections and readers can exist, but only one write transaction can write a database at a time; the exact reader/writer overlap depends on journaling mode.
Write contention occurs when connections compete for that writer slot or incompatible locks. A busy result reports that the needed access could not be obtained under the current conditions.

Keep write transactions short and avoid unrelated slow work while holding them. A configured busy timeout or appropriate bounded retry can tolerate brief contention, but failures still need handling and transaction-level retry may be necessary.
Waiting and retries do not add concurrent writers or guarantee a successful attempt; sustained competing write demand can justify a different access arrangement or client-server database.

Rollback journaling records original page contents so an interrupted change can be undone while updates modify the database file. WAL appends changes to a separate log before they are later incorporated into the database file.
WAL readers use a stable view while a writer appends, allowing readers and a writer to overlap; WAL still allows only one writer at a time.
A checkpoint transfers eligible WAL changes into the main database. Readers holding old views can limit checkpoint completion or log reuse, allowing the WAL to grow.
WAL coordination depends on supported shared-memory/file locking on the same host; placing an actively shared WAL database on an arbitrary network filesystem is not a general multi-server solution.
criticalMisconceptions: One writer means only one connection or reader is possible.
A busy timeout guarantees every transaction succeeds.
WAL enables multiple simultaneous writers.
Checkpointing means an active WAL file can always be deleted safely.

questions.question: Define index and query plan. For a frequent query that filters by owner and orders rows by time, describe how to choose a candidate access path and inspect EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN. Why can a table scan still be reasonable, and what are the costs of additional indexes even though the database is local? What responsibilities remain when SQLite has no separate server? Explain permissions, schema migrations and tested backups. Why is copying only the main database file during active WAL writes unsafe, and how does a supported backup mechanism or verified quiescent state address the problem? Does having a file prove you can restore correctly?
criteria: An index is an additional access structure that can avoid scanning or sorting all rows; a plan describes how the query will access its data.
Match candidate index columns/order to filters and requested ordering, inspect EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, and measure representative data and queries to see whether less work is done.
Scans can be preferable for small tables or broad queries, and the planner need not use an index simply because it exists.
Local execution still consumes CPU, I/O and memory. Indexes use disk space and add maintenance to writes, so they are not free or universally beneficial.
The application/operator must manage access permissions, storage capacity, schema changes and recovery even without a separate database service.
Schema migrations change the stored structure and must be coordinated with application versions and active access; a file-based deployment does not make incompatible changes harmless.

Active WAL state can contain committed data absent from the main file; blindly copying that file alone can miss required state or make an inconsistent backup. Use a supported consistent backup method or establish a correctly quiescent complete state.
Retain backups according to recovery needs and test restoration and application usability. File existence alone does not establish backup consistency or recovery time.
criticalMisconceptions: Local database queries do not need performance analysis.
Every additional index makes every operation faster.
Copying the live main database file alone is always a complete safe backup.
No database server means no operational responsibilities.

questions.question: Compare a single-host application with short occasional writes to several application servers making sustained concurrent writes to shared data. Explain an SQLite choice or rejection for each, addressing locality, one-writer behavior, WAL limits, constraints, queries and backups. Which measurements or missing requirements would you verify before committing to the choice?
criteria: SQLite can fit the single-host local workload because it avoids a separate service, provided its write contention and storage behavior meet requirements; it is not restricted to a single human user.
Sustained writes from multiple servers favor evaluating a client-server database; WAL does not remove the one-writer limit or supply automatic network replication/synchronization.
Either choice still requires explicit data rules, correct transactions, measured query/index behavior and a consistent tested backup/recovery process.
Verify actual concurrent write duration/rate, busy behavior, deployment and data-sharing needs, query latency and recovery targets; avoid deciding from an arbitrary row-count or user-count threshold.
criticalMisconceptions: WAL makes SQLite a distributed multi-writer server.
Choosing SQLite eliminates backup and data-integrity work.
